findings.detail: I recounted both waves with my own Python/SQL against drive.sqlite and the claimed counts hold. Wave 2 (parked + OneDrive-Import prefix): 102,703 candidates out of 122,166 files that have an md5 hash, totalling 124.27 GB (decimal; 115.74 GiB). That includes 544 zero-byte files; the other 102,159 are backed by a twin. Wave 3 (unsorted): 3,410 candidates out of 23,074 files with an md5 hash, totalling 24.40 GB (22.72 GiB). That includes 5 zero-byte files; the other 3,405 are backed by a twin. None of the 3,566 ids trashed in wave 1 fall in either wave, and no candidate lost its kept twin to the wave 1 trash. Read-only throughout: no dry-run, no Drive calls, no trash_dry CSV left behind.

Single-copy exposure: 68,221 wave 2 candidates (78.05 GB, 66% of the wave) have exactly one kept twin. That is 66,917 of 78,935 distinct md5+size keys. In wave 3 the figure is 1,834 candidates (2.29 GB), or 1,141 of 2,157 keys. After these waves run, that one twin is the last copy. Any later cleanup of the kept folders, especially the _STALLED and _DONE project folders, would then delete data for good. Mark those twin ids, or the folders holding them, as do-not-trash before any later cleanup touches them.

Concentration in wave 2: for 80,618 candidates, every kept twin sits in a single 3-level folder. The top five are 01_PROJECTS/_STALLED (35,752 files, 5.62 GB), 01_PROJECTS/_DONE (18,700, 0.59 GB), 10_ARCHIVE/PERSONAL (17,023, 12.95 GB), 10_ARCHIVE/2021 (2,812, 1.26 GB) and 10_ARCHIVE/2026 (1,512, 0.20 GB). Counting candidates with at least one twin in a folder, the order is _STALLED 50,574, PERSONAL 33,900, _DONE 32,404. Holding the only copies in _STALLED and _DONE is risky, because folders with those names tend to be cleanup targets themselves.

Backup-word paths: as the task specified (the full word list, including 'archive'), 23,285 wave 2 candidates (22.62 GB) and 1,598 wave 3 candidates (2.20 GB) have only kept twins whose paths contain backup-like words. That number is inflated because the kept zone 'archive' lives under 10_ARCHIVE, so the word 'archive' matches almost everything there. With 'archive' dropped and 'old' matched as a whole word, the counts fall to 287 files (5.54 GB, mostly large files) in wave 2 and 14 files (about 0 GB) in wave 3. Check those 287 wave 2 files by hand, or exclude them, before the wave runs.

Concentration in wave 3: for 2,002 candidates, every kept twin sits in a single 3-level folder. The top five are 10_ARCHIVE/Institutional & Career Archives (1,154 files, 1.14 GB), 10_ARCHIVE/2026 (393, 0.01 GB), 09_PRO_DEV/Athletic Performance & Sports Science (165, 7.05 GB), 01_PROJECTS/_STALLED (131) and 04_RESEARCH/_INBOX (77, 0.06 GB). 04_RESEARCH/_INBOX is an inbox and may be cleaned later: 1,333 candidates (15.10 GB) have at least one twin there.

Recent files: no candidate in either wave was modified on or after 2026-10-01. The newest candidate dates are 2026-06-23 (wave 2) and 2026-09-10 (wave 3). The scope does contain newer files (7 in wave 2, 29 in wave 3), but none of them has a kept twin, so the script would skip them. They may be live work, so it is worth knowing they sit in hidden zones.

Script behaviour (read, not imported): it checks only the first 3 indexed twins against live Drive. If those 3 are gone it skips the file rather than trashing it, so it fails safe, but it can understate how many files it trashes. Its resume log is per zone (trash_log_<zone>.csv), separate from the 10-22 log. Google Docs and Sheets without an md5 (16,885 such files in these two zones) are never candidates.

Duplicates inside the waves: 12,195 wave 2 md5 keys and 654 wave 3 keys have more than one candidate copy. Every copy goes on trust in the same kept twin or twins, so each of those twins carries more than one file.

findings.detail: I checked a random sample of 60 files live on Drive through the gws CLI (seed 20261022), using only 'gws drive files get'. All 60 passed. Wave 2: 40 of 40 ok. Wave 3: 20 of 20 ok. For every sampled file, the file itself was not trashed, its md5 and size matched the index, and its parent folder had not changed. Every sampled file also had a kept-zone twin that was not trashed, matched on md5 and size, and was still in its indexed parent folder. No file failed, so there are no bad ids to report.
I recomputed the candidate sets from drive.sqlite and they match the claimed figures exactly. Wave 2: 102,703 files, 124.27 GB. Wave 3: 3,410 files, 24.40 GB.

Zero-byte files get trashed without any twin check, by design: 544 in wave 2 and 5 in wave 3. None of them came up in the random sample, so they were not checked live. The only live check on these is that the file is unchanged. That is low risk because an empty file holds no data, but if a folder depends on an empty file existing (for example a marker or placeholder), that file would still go to the trash.

The script tries at most 3 indexed twins per file. If all 3 have moved, the file is skipped (skip_no_live_twin) rather than trashed. That fails safe. It may leave some true duplicates behind, which a re-index would pick up.

The wave 2 prefix has no trailing slash, so it could in principle match sibling folders with longer names. I checked: it matches 0 such folders. No native Google Docs/Sheets file matches a twin, so none are at risk. I made no changes and did not run trash_twins.py at all, so no trash_dry CSV was written (0 such files in drive-index/). My temporary verify script in /tmp has been deleted.

findings.detail: The run cannot be stopped once started (lines 105-106). ex.map submits every item at once: about 102.7k for wave 2. On Ctrl-C or any worker exception, the with-block runs shutdown(wait=True) without cancel_futures, so every queued item still goes through one() and still gets trashed. kill -9 is the only brake. Wave 1 was 3.5k items, so this never mattered. Fix: put ex.shutdown(cancel_futures=True) in a try/finally, or check for a stop file at the top of one().

The candidate's ancestry is not rechecked (line 80). same() confirms the file is still in its indexed parent folder id. It does not confirm that folder is still inside _PARKED_COPIES or 99_UNSORTED. If Eric drags a parked or unsorted subfolder into the ladder after the index build (10-22 17:55), its files keep their parent id, pass the check, and are trashed. No bytes are lost, because the twin survives, but a folder he deliberately rescued gets emptied. trash_review.py did not have this gap: it required the flat _TO_REVIEW id itself as the parent. Fix: rebuild the index just before each wave, or get the parent folder's chain and require it still sits under the prefix or zone root. Twins have the same gap in reverse (only the immediate parent is checked), but trashed ancestors are caught, since Drive's trashed flag covers files whose parent folder was trashed.

--zone computers is accepted with only a printed warning (lines 27-29). Until that wave is approved, require an explicit flag such as --backups-off-confirmed, or remove computers from choices. The machine and unresolved zones are correctly impossible to target.

The script never checks for a second parent. A legacy file with two parents, one hidden and one kept, would pass (the indexed parent is in its parents list), and trashing it would also remove it from the kept folder. The index stores only the first parent. A live sample found none: 150 wave-2 and 150 wave-3 candidates plus their first twins all had exactly 1 parent. Cheap guard: require len(meta['parents']) == 1 for the candidate.

Resume with --limit stalls. The limit is applied at line 64, before the done filter at line 77, so a resumed run with --limit N re-walks the same first N items as 'already'. 'order by folder' is also not a total order, so the slice can shift between runs; add ', id' to the order by. Also, a truncated last CSV row after a crash makes r[1] raise IndexError on resume. That fails safe, by crashing. Dry-run logs append and are never cleaned up.

Kept twins that are themselves backups or archive copies. The twins always survive, because the script can only target hidden zones and twins come only from kept zones. But after waves 2 and 3 these locations hold the only Drive copy, so any later cleanup of 10_ARCHIVE or of report-C folders must treat them as originals. Parked: 22,997 files (16.4 GB) have twins only in the archive zone (10_ARCHIVE outside _PARKED_COPIES), and 434 files (6.9 GB) have all twins inside kept-zone backup-looking folders from backup_folders.csv. Unsorted: 1,588 files (1.6 GB) archive-only, and 13 in backup-looking folders. Separately, the top-level folder 'Mark for deletion' (root_other, a kept zone) holds the first twin for 20 parked and 9 unsorted candidates. 2 and 2 of those have all their twins there (under 1 MB). Eric should decide whether that folder really counts as kept.

Zero-byte files: 544 parked and 5 unsorted files are trashed with no twin required, only a live check of size 0 and the empty md5. Same policy as wave 1, by design. Only the file names are lost, for example placeholder or marker files.

Checked and safe. The LIKE escaping is correct: backslash is escaped first, then % and _, and escape '\' is valid SQL. The prefix matched 0 sibling folders, every match being the exact folder or a subfolder. id is the primary key, so there are 0 duplicate ids and no file can appear twice. A twin can never be a candidate, because twins come only from kept zones and candidates only from the chosen hidden zone. Twins are keyed on (md5, size), which is stricter than wave 1's md5-only. Sizes are stored as integers in all 620,825 rows, and Drive's string size is cast with int(). All md5s are lowercase text. gws returning None, an error dict, or a missing size all fall through to a skip (size -1 never matches); none leads to a trash. A failed update is logged as 'error', and on retry the file shows trashed, so it is skipped. Google Docs and shortcuts have no md5, so they are excluded. The 7 md5-bearing 'shortcuts' are Windows .lnk files, which are real files. The index lists only files Eric owns, so a twin cannot belong to someone else. CSV writes and counts are under a lock. The selection matches the claims exactly: wave 2 has 102,703 candidates (124.3 GB) of 122,166 md5 files, and wave 3 has 3,410 (24.4 GB) of 23,074. For 97% of wave-2 candidates the twin's last folder name matches the candidate's, so the twins look like the reorganized ladder originals and not a second mirror.
